two hon. members of this House, when it was suggested that they had been implicated in dealing in supplies for the Militia Department, stood up and indignantly denied the accusation. We know what happened, we know the investigation that took place in the Public Accounts Committee, and we know that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) found it incumbent upon himself to read both of these hon .gentlemen out of the party and out of this House. Here is the language used by the right hon. gentleman on that occasion:
An delt me say now, for the benefit of Parliament, and particularly for the Information of persons throughout this country who may be concerned in selling supplies or materials to the Government account, if any man in Canada, be he Conservative or Liberal, purposes to commit any fraud or imposition upon the Government and people of this country, or to be concerned in any attempt for that purpose, especially in connection with the war vote, he should remember that there are courts of justice in this country and that the doors of the penitentiary are opening for every person who commits such an offense.
I think the Prime Minister stated when he addressed the House the other day that there had been some three prosecutions and one conviction for frauds committed upon the Government'. I was not aware that there were three prosecutions. I am aware that there was one prosecution in Regina a few months ago and that a conviction resulted from that prosecution. If v others have taken place in the criminal courts, I am not aware of it. Further, the Prime Minister said, speaking of the case of the late member for Kings, Nova Scotia.
But I am hound to say that his (Mr. Foster's) explanation to me of his undertaking the duty and his explanation-if it could be called an explanation-of his failure to supervise in the most careful manner the expenditure of that money and to bring back to the Government an exact account, with vouchers of every dollar that has been expended must he regarded as far-from satisfactory.
Therefore, in respect of the honourable members for Carleton, and in respect to the honourable member for Kings, N.S., I feel that I owe , it as a duty to the Government of which I am the head of the party, of which in Federal affairs I am the leader, and to this House, and to this county, to express, as I do here express, my firm disapproval of their conduct in respect of the matters which have been under investigation by the Public Accounts Committee.
That is the declaration which, I believe, resulted in these two hon. gentlemen sending in their -resignationis to your predecessor, Mr. Speaker. It is well known that the counties of Carleton, Ont., and Kings, N.S., are unrepresented at the present time

in the House of Commons. But the Con

servative party in Kings, N.S., met in annual meeting a few weeks ago, and I will read for the information of this House wliat the Conservative party in Kings County thinks of the repudiation of their member by the Prime Minister:
Kentville, January 6-The annual meeting of the Kings county Liberal-Conservative association was held this afternoon at the court house. After the usual routine business was finished, the president invited DeWitt Foster to address the meeting. At the close of a powerful address on the war and Canada's participation in it, the following resolution was moved by Councillor C. R. Nichols, seconded by .Councillor W. A. Reid, and carried amid three cheers and a tiger:
'* Resolved that the Liberal-Conservative Association of Kings county, in annual meeting assembled, take this opportunity to express its appreciation of the untiring efforts put forth by A. DeWitt Faster, in the interests of the county and to record its unbounded confidence in his integrity and ability to successfully and creditably represent Kings county in federal affairs."
Now we have the pot fairly bristling over. The Prime Minister, in indignant tones, read the member for Kings out of the party last year and the Conservative press of this country claimed great credit for him for his sturdy manliness, in determining to rid the Conservative party of all grafters and wrong-doers and for having actually read Mr. Foster out ol the party. There has been no election held in Kings but I understand that if an election is called the Conservative party in Kings, living' up to their resolution, will name Mr. A. DeWitt Foster as their candidate because they consider him good enough to support this Government in Parliament. What ground have I for making that assumption? There is a precedent foj it. We know what happened in the province of New Brunswick a fe v years ago. We know that Mr. J. K. Flemming, the Premier of New Brunswick, was the subject of accusations in regard to certain peculations in which he indulged in respect to the owners of timber limits of that province. He was deposed from the leadership of his party in provincial affairs, he was driven out of the public life of the province, but the Conservative party in federal affairs, a very short time afterwards, named him their candidate in Car-leton county for the House of Commons because they thought that, although he was not good enough for provincial politics, he was good enough to associate with the ministers who form this Government. 1 cite this instance to show the insincerity
10*
of certain elements supporting the Conservative party in this Dominion. Recalling the professions made by the First Minister and his promise to prosecute until he had landed in the penitentiary those who had been guilty of wrong-doing, I would not say that the situation of this country was so critical, but in view of what has taken place in the past, in view of what we are sure will take place in the future, the only safety, the only assurance that the people can possibly have that, this Government will carry on more economically, more honestly and more in the public interest the affairs with which they have been entrusted is in the appointment of a committee of this House for the purpose of investigating every dollar of public expenditure, not only in respect to shells, but in respect to supplies of every kind and description purchased by the Government during the last eighteen months. Not until this report is presented to Parliament and the Government prove by their actions that they mean what they say, will suspicion be allayed and confidence be restored.

On the Orders of the Day:

I desire to speak on a question of privilege. I had not the pleasure of being in the House yesterday when my hon. friend the Solicitor General spoke, but I observe that he regretted rry absence, and pointed out that he had been present while I spoke. I can assure my hon. friend that my absence was not caused by any want of desire to hear him. I had understood that my hon. friend was to follow me, 'but the distinguished and able debater from North Essex (Mr. Wilcox) was put up so as to give my hon. friend breathing time. If I had known my hon. friend was going to speak yesterday I should have made my engagements to suit. My hon. friend made an extraordinary statement yesterday with reference to the shell matter, which I think it is my duty to call to the attention of the House. It appears on page 129 of Hansard, as follows:
Here is the way it is put upon Hansard, doubtless for distribution throughout the length and breadth of Canada:
I was quoting from the speech of Mr. Thomas:
" That must be considered, and I may tell you that the cost of shells in Canada has been higher than in competitive countries. It is complained that fat orders have gone to the United States, but I can assure you that a big slice will be reserved for Canada as long as [DOT] the price is fairly satisfactory. The prices so far have been far higher than in the United States or in Great Britain."
Then, the Solicitor General proceeds to say:
Strange that that should be the way that it appears in Hansard in the speech of the hon. member for St. John, when the words in the quotation from which he read distinctly say " that the prices have been higher than in the United States."
The fair inference from that is that I read an extract-to this House which was altered in Hansard.
No, no.
-at my instance, I presume, for the purpose of being circulated broadcast throughout Canada.
No, no.

The fair inference from
the words of the Solicitor General is that I read what purported to be an extract from the speech of Mr. Thomas, and that it was altered in Hansard for distribution throughout the length and breadth of Canada, so as to give a faulty impression of what Mr. Thomas had said. The extract as I read it to the House was seot to Hansard word for word, without lamy alteration. I did not see any member of the

Hansard staff upon the subject; I had no communication directly or indirectly with any member of the staff, and the error which occurred occurred in Hansard and without any fault of mine. As I read the extract, so I sent it out to Hansard with other memoranda for which the Han,-sard reporter asked. I noticed the mistake when I read over my speech in the Unrevised Hansard, and I immediately corrected it, striking out the word " far," and sent the correction for the Revised Hansard, before my attention wlals called to the remarks of the Solicitor General.
With regard to the matter of the purchase of submarines, my. hon. friend, veTy unfairly I thought, sought to convey the impression that when I made the statement to the House that to my surprise certain matters had been left uninvestigated, that certain questions had been left unanswered, I at that time had in my possession a copy of the evidence taken by the commission; because my hon. friend is reported to have made this statement, which appears on page 137 of Hansard;
I quote from the evidence. I am informed that the evidence has been handed to the Opposition-at all events to the leader of the Opposition-and, consequently should be at the disposal of his followers in the same way as it was at mine, which was only yesterday.
Now, Sir, the day when I spoke on the subject of submarines was the day before my hon. friend had himself obtained the evidence.
What I said was that 1 had received it yesterday.

I had not seen the evidence; I had not heard of it, and I presumed it w-o-ulH not be (available for anybody until the official report was brought down and submitted to the House. That is the time when we have a right to expect the evidence and when I expected that it would be brought down, and I very much suspect that, after I had made my remarks with regard to the submarines, my hon. friend took pains to get the evidence, and in all probability he had a copy of it sent to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, but it was done after I had made my remarks.
Mr. hon. friend did me an injustice in another respect when he sought to convey the impression that I had been guilty of very great unfairness in not .quoting correctly the examination by Mr. Thompson before the commissioner with regard to the test.
I rise to a point of order. This is no question of privilege whatever. The hon. gentleman is endeavouring to make a reply to my speech. He is distinctly out of order.	[DOT]

Not at all. The hon. gentleman went on to attack me. He stated that I had been guilty of conduct which in truth he could not describe as* the conduct of a gentleman. Before he closed, it is true, he said he had made remarks which he had not intended to make,, and which were unparliamentary or might be unparliamentary.

I am addressing His
Honour now.

Order. I, understand
that the hon. member for St. John-is speaking in order to correct some remarks which were made by the hon. Solicitor General, and, according to the practice followed in this House, as can be seen in Bourinot, I think that the hon. member for St." John can proceed with his remarks.

My hon. friend sought
to convey the impression that I knew when I made those remarks that the commissioner had inquired very carefully into the test which had been made of the submarines, and he quoted from the evidence, as reported on page 139 of Hansard. My hon. friend sought to convey the impression that Mr. Paterson had stated what the test was. An examination of the evidence as submitted by my hon. friend shows that no such test as the hon. member speaks of was-made, and therefore it shows that his attack on me as misrepresenting the test is entirely unfounded. My hon. friend proceeded to-say that there was evidence that there were tests, and one would infer from his remarks-that the test required the submarines to be weighted down to the extent of 5,000 tons. If we read the evidence, we find that Mr. Paterson only mentions 5,000 tons as an illustration of what the contract might require. When I call the attention of the House to the fact that the total displacement of the submarines is only 313 tons each, lion, members will see how unfair my hon. friend was when he said that there had been a full examination as to the actual tests that had been made, and that I was-unfair in my remarks.

Mr. BERNARD R. HEPBURN (Prince Edward):	Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. On the 18th instant, the * hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) made certain observations in this House regarding my connection with shell contracts. On that particular evening I was not present in the Chamber, and I regret very much that the hon. gentleman did not tell me he was going to speak in regard to myself, or I would have made an extra effort to be present. On the following day I was out of the city and had not had an opportunity to bring the matter to the attention of the House until to-day. On page 78 of Hansard the hon. member for St. John is reported as saying:
People came here from all parts of Canada, politicians, canvassing agents, committee men, influential people from different sections of the country, all clamouring for orders for shells, and among others my good friend the gentleman to whom I have referred, the member fo-r Prince Edward County, obtained for his company a- large order. His company is not engaged in the manufacture of steel. He owns a.plaiyng mill, I understand, and is engaged in the manufacture of wooden ware. I could understand if he had limited his application to shell boxes that would have been a worthy ambition which could have been fulfilled by the utilizing of his machinery. But he got an order for shells, and the people of Picton naturally supposed it would mean the creation of a local industry which might have justified him in pressing upon the Shell Committee and the Minister of Militia that he was right in using his influence to secure this order so as to enable a steel plant to be erected in my hon. friend's home town.
It is quite true that the firm of Hepburn Brothers, Limited, obtained an order for the forging and machining of shells. My brothers and myself, and my father before me, operated steamboats on the Great Lakes and river St. Lawrence for many years. In connection with that busi-
.! \XUAHY 21, 1916
ness we 'maintained aind operated a machine shop at Picton. We have known General Bertram, formerly chairman of the Shell Committee, for many, many years, and have transacted to our mutual satisfaction no inconsiderable amount of business with his firm. We applied to the Shell Committee for a contract for the forging and machining of shells. We were awarded a contract, not because I was a member of Parliament, but because General Bertram and the committee knew that we had a plant and could complete any contract we undertook. We believed at that time that, with certain modifications and additions, we could utilize our plant at Picton. After having obtained the order-at a price in the fixing of which we had no part, hut which was at the uniform rate given to all producers of shells for the same work at that time in Eastern Canada-we discovered, on the report of a competent engineer from Montreal, that our plant at Picton could not economically be utilized in fulfilling the contract. I then obtained further expert advice, as a result of which, having regard to the point at .which billets were being manufactured, and having regard also to the fact that .Montreal was the labour market of Eastern Canada, we located the plant at Montreal, where we have since forged and machined shells to the satisfaction of the committee and its inspectors. 1 regret to say that we were unsuccessful in securing a box order, though from time to time we waited upon the Shell Commitee. I sincerely trust that when other orders are to be placed, it will not be forgotten that the firm of Hepburn Brothers have a planing mill in Picton, and that some orders will be turned our way.
The hon. member for St. John continued:
But he .got an order for shells and took it to Montreal, antf the shells are being made there now in the east end of Montreal by another concern, the member for Prince Edward County being the go-between or the. middleman in connection with the transaction.
These statements are absolutely incorrect. I am a new member in this Parliament. The hon. gentleman who made that statement is an old parliamentarian, and 1 resent very strongly the imputation that there was anything dishonest or dishonourable in connection with my relation to this contract.
Will my hon. friend pardon me a moment?	y
Order.

I wish to say right
here that I made no suggestion-and would he sorry to say I made any suggestion- of fraud on the part of my hon. friend. I should like to disabuse his mind in that respect.

I understood that the
Shell Committee was letting contracts for the Imperial Government. A firm of which I am a member and a director has obtained an order for the forging and machining of shells. That work is being done by that firm, and 1 have been and am giving to the business of the company as careful attention as it is possible for me to do. I have made inquiry, and I have been unable to ascertain that there is any rule or custom in this House or in the Senate that prevents a member of either body from being a shareholder or director or officer of a company or corporation holding contracts with the Imperial Government. If I violated any rule or custom, I at least, have the satisfaction of knowing that others are* similarly situated. It must be known to the hon. member for St. John, as it is to most members of this House, that no inconsiderable number of the members of both parties, in the Commons as well as in the Senate, are interested in companies of that, kind, as shareholders, directors, and officers. I trust that one with the long parliamentary experience of the hon. member for St. John will at least do me the justice of withdrawing the imputation which he has made against me on the floor of this House.

I have too much
respect and too much regard for my hon.' friend to be willing even to appear to do him an injustice. I was not finding any fault with him-not at all. The Minister of Labour may laugh, but it was with gentlemen occupying positions similar to that occupied by him-members of this Government-that I was finding fault, and with the Shell Committee. I dealt with my hon. friend's firm as a firm that was not engaged in the manufacture of steel, my point being' that tlie Shell Committee had given orders to many people who had no plant, no machinery, and no experience in steel-manufacturing work. I made a statement also which my hon. friend says is true: that the work was not established in Picton, but in the east end of Montreal. As I explained, my hon. friend denies only the statement that I made that he was a go-between or middleman. If my hon. friend says that that is not the position he

occupied, I cheerfully accept his statement, and withdraw the statement which I made to the effect that he was a go-between or middleman. But that does not at all interfere with the argument which I was making: that the Government and the Shell Committee were to be condemned for the practice that they pursued of letting out shell contracts to people who had no plant capable of manufacturing such munitions.

And here I may interrupt the reading of this article to say that, within the last few days, that view has been strongly supported by Lord Derby. The article proceeds:
If that be so, what motive will the self-governing dominions have to draw closer their relations with the Mother Country? While they had to count with a war with so aggressive and so powerful a country as Germany it was natural that they should desire not only to give assistance to the Mother Country, but also to secure the protection of the British fleet for their overseas communications. But what need will they have for the protection of the British fleet if they can reasonably count upon peace for half a century? Similarly, we ourselves will come out of the war loaded with debt. Our main thought will be to reduce that debt as rapidly as possible, to find means of keeping up our revenue, and especially of pushing our trade in every direction, so that we may pay off at least 100 millions of debt per annum. If that is to be our main preoccupation, is it likely that either the public or ministers will trouble much about drawing closer the relations with the daughter countries? We shall retain for them the same affection as now. But we shall -comfort ourselves that if the day of distress comes they will prove to us as they are proving . now, " that blood is thicker than water," and we shall put off to a time of greater leisure the reorganization of the Epipire.
*On second thought, and perhaps after reading that article of Sir George Paish, the Toronto News in a further discussion of the subject was not so cocksure of the position which it had taken in the first instance, and in a quotation from an editorial of the News, reproduced in the Ottawa Citizen of October 14, 1915, I read this:
On crossing the Atlantic he-
That is the right hon. the Prime Minister

	.
[DOT]-was invited to take his seat in the Imperial Cabinet-an honour never before enjoyed by a Dominion statesman. The incident was full of meaning for the future. Sir Robert Borden's demand on the part of the Dominion for a voice in Imperial affairs is in the way of being realized.
The first article in the News said it had been realized.
Now, the right hon. the Prime Minister, so far as I know, has not given the public of this country any information on the subject. The only incidental reference that has fallen from his lips on the subject since his return from England, that has come under my notice in any event, is contained in a speech which he delivered some time last month -before the Canadian Club in New York. In the course of that
4 p.m. speech, The Farmers Sun of Toronto represents the right hon. gentleman in its issue of December 29 last, as having said this:

It is realized that the great policies and questions which concern and govern the issues of peace and war cannot in future be assumed by the people of the British Islands alone.
And commenting on that somewhat delphic utterance, The Farmers Sun said:
The proposal implies of course either distrust of British diplomacy in the past or a crusader's impulse to bear arms against the world. While it is doubtful whether the colonies can by any arrangement whatever or by any menace of arms become influential in European politics, it is not doubtful that to make the attempt, however feebly, they must permanently commit themselves to share the burdens of European militarism. They will never be able to speak again of voluntary participation in Europe's wars.
About the same time as the right hon. the Prime Minister spoke before the Canadian Club in New York, the matter was practically given its quietus in the British House of Commons. On December 22, 1915, the Ottawa Citizen published this cable despatch :
London, December 21.-The Premier in the House of Commons to-night was asked whether, in view of the share taken by the dominions in various theatres of war, he would include representatives of Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, in the British Cabinet without increasing its size.
Mr. Asquith :	I don't think the proposal is
practicable. The Colonial Secretary has already intimated to the dominions that they will be consulted in connection with terms of peace, and that the Government will warmly welcome any Prime Minister who finds it convenient to come here to discuss fully and frankly questions of Imperial policy.
This would show, according to Mr. Asquith, that a warm welcome awaits any Prime Minister of the overseas dominions, but no seat in the Cabinet. Thai, Mr. Speaker, makes it quite evident that so far as our Imperial relations are concerned, they were not changed by the attendance of the right hon. the Prime Minister at the British Cabinet meeting last summer. It further makes plain that the original dictum of Mr. Asquith still stands, namely, that the. British Government cannot share its responsibilities for the issues of peace and war with any of the overseas dominions.
In his speech yesterday, my hon. friend who sits beside me to the right (Hon. Frank Oliver) urged upon the Government the necessity of new and larger action in the care of wounded and disabled soldiers. My hon. friend was listened to, with profound attention, and in my judgment he never was more convincing than he was in that speech of yesterday. He fully deserved the compliment that was paid him by my

hon. friend the Solicitor General. In speaking as he did, the hon. member for Edmonton spoke not at all from a sense of the parental sacrifices that he has had the privilege and the pride of making, but rather from that sturdy sense of public duty which has always distinguished him as one of the people's representatives. Naturally, in my case his words fell upon receptive ears and if any word of mine can add force to what the hon. gentleman said yesterday I would appeal to the Government to lose not one minute in applying themselves to the task of revising the schedule upon which allotments are to be made in the future to wounded and disabled soldiers.
I say, further, that while we have voted hundreds of millions, this House and this country are quite willing to vote hundreds of millions more in order that a proud, willing and generous people may discharge its full duty towards the men who have faced the Grim Reaper and have given the best that was in them in defence of their native land and the British Empire. The Government cannot act too quickly in this matter, and in acting they may be assured of the unanimous and hearty support of the gentlemen on this side of the House. As my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has said, all these expenses, no matter of what character, should be borne by the Government, and if the Government, in performing the task which my hon. friend has suggested, and which I also urge-upon them, could do something to stop the mad rage that has seized upon a certain portion of the community for soliciting subscriptions for -this, that and the other thing, they would confer a Very real and lasting benefit upon a worried and harassed portion of the business and professional community. Parliament, I repeat, should provide all these funds, and I am sure that both sides of the House will combine to support the Government in whatever new measures they may propose.
In his criticism of war expenditures my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) urged upon the Government the necessity of holding a speedy enquiry into all these expenditures. A similar request has been made by every hon. gentleman who has spoken from this side of the House, and all these gentlemen wer6 merely voicing a demand that has become general on the part of the public. Let me illustrate, Mr. Speaker, how general that demand is, and perhaps I can best do that by citing certain facts connected with the correspondence that took place in the fall of 1914 between the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the right hon. the Prime Minister. It will be recalled that my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) made an inquiry in this House on the 29th of March last regarding the receipt of that correspondence by the Prime Minister or by any member of the Government. On that occasion the Prime Minister was not in his seat, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was leading the House, said that he had no knowledge of the correspondence, but would bring the enquiry to the attention of the Prime Minister, when a decision would be reached as to whether it could be brought down to the House. That was on the 29th of March. On the 8th of April last the matter again came up in the House, upon a motion by my hon. friend from South Renfrew, which was adopted by the House. The motion read as follows:
For a copy of all correspondence that has taken place since August 4 last between any official of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and the Prime Minister, the Acting Prime Minister or any member of the Government or any department thereof.
On that date, April 8, a short discussion ensued. The Prime Minister stated that he had received a communication from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, but that he understood the Canadian Manufacturers' Association regarded it as of a confidential character. Later on he added that after communicating with the association he would bring the correspondence down if they had no objection. Another inquiry was made in regard to this correspondence-on April 13, 1915, by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) on behalf of the-hon. member for South Renfrew, who was absent at the time, and in reply to that inquiry the Prime Minister said that he had communicated with the gentleman who had written him the letter but had not yet received a reply.	.
Now, Sir, there is something extraordinary about all this. As I have stated, the-first inquiry about this matter was made in the House on March 29. On the following day, March 30, 1915, an interview with Mr. G. M. Murray, Secretary of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, was published in the Toronto Star; and, speaking with reference to this correspondence, Mr. Murray said that it was not confidential and that the Prime Minister could bring it down if he pleased. About a week later the Toronto Globe appended to its report of

* a. further discussion in this House about the matter a foot-note in these terms:
Mr. G. M. Murray, secretary of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, in an interview on March 30, while not admitting that any letters of protest had been written to the Government in regard to the above, was quoted as saying, " Any letters that were written were to the Premier, and he can make them public if he chooses."	'
As you will observe, Mr. Speaker, there is a very sharp conflict between the statement of the Prime Minister and that oi Mr. Murray. I make no comment on that. I do not want to introduce anything harsh or controversial into the discussion. It is not necessary for me to make any comment at all; the facts speak for themselves. The matter was further dealt with in an editorial in the Toronto Globe on April 17 last, two days after this House prorogued. I will quote some paragraphs from that editorial :
Why did the Prime Minister arrange for the prorogation of Parliament without first bringing down the war-graft correspondence between himself and the executive of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association? That correspondence was called for again and again, and yet again, within the past four weeks. Parliament had a right to it. It is of intense public interest. Its interest is measured not only by its intrinsic merits, but also by the studied and persistent efforts of the Government to keep it secret. Why is it kept secret by the Prime Minister?
That correspondence, as known to other members of the Cabinet, deals very plainly and in interesting detail with important lines of war-graft not investigated and not even mentioned 'in the committees or before the House. A series of typical graft cases in several provinces, and covering various types of exploitation by different orders of favoured " middlemen," are described. Names and places and dates are given. Circumstances are recited. Evidence both illuminating and condemnatory is outlined. It is all in the hands of the Prime Minister. Why was it not submitted to Parliament?
That correspondence dates back to the early days of the war-contract scandals. It presents facts. It appeals for Investigation. It warns against delay. Why was it unheeded?
Later on in the same article, referring to the Prime Minister's attitude in the House, the editorial goes on:
He talked about the correspondence being "confidential.'' He professed willingness to lay it before Parliament if granted "Permission." He needed no man's permission. Why did he not do it?
The correspondence was public, not private. It was between a public body and the Prime Minister. It dealt solely with matters of high and serious public moment. Weeks ago the Executive of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association declared publicly that " the Premier .may publish it if he chooses." Why did Sir 
Robert Borden not choose to lay that very important correspondence before Parliament?
Is it true that the publication of that correspondence might clash very harshly with the Prime Minister's grave-toned condemnation of Garland and Foster, and might contradict very emphatically, and utterly discount, all his own protestations about war-grafters and middlemen? Why was not his zeal for Governmental honesty, his condemnation of barefaced robbery, his respect for the doors of the penitentiary, and his enthusiasm for political purity as professed solemnly on Thursday-why did all these fine qualities slumber through September and October? Had he heeded the warnings of his friends In the Manufacturers' Association then would two of his supporters in Parliament be accursed as war-graft scapegoats now ? Why did he mock at those warnings ? That is the people's question to the Premier.
WTiy ?
This matter was regarded so seriously by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association that special reference was made to it in the report presented at the annual meeting of the executive committee of that association held in the city of Toronto on the 9th of June last. So seriously did the association Tegard this matter that it took [DOT]the trouble to -hand out official reports of the proceedings of the annual meeting to the several newspapers. In these reports so handed out by the executive, special attention was drawn to one important paragraph in the executive committee's report. That paragraph, as reproduced in the Citizen of June last, reads as follows:
Less than a month later, on October 23-
That is, in the year 1914

Less than a month later, on October 23, a letter was addressed to the Premier, pointing out that the method of handling war orders was giving rise to ,a good deal of dissatisfaction. He was informed that, making all due allowance for the fact that some manufacturers might not have had the necessary equipment, and that others might not have been able to guarantee satisfactory deliveries, it was apparently true that some had more than their share of business, while others had gone without. In some quarters the impression seemed to prevail that war material could not be sold to the Government on its merits, but only through influence, and it was accordingly suggested to the Premier that the business should be thrown wider open, and placed as far as possible with manufacturers or producers direct, instead of through middlemen, thus insuring competitive prices, and at the same time giving the Government the satisfaction of dealing with responsible parties.
Then, Sir, in order to emphasize the warning that they had sent out to the Prime Minister, the executive committee go on in their report to explain why they did that, and they furnish by their explanation a key to practically thev whole

of the correspondence. I quote again from the Citizen report of the 10th of June last:
The words of the executive committee's report, showing the motive behind the explanation of the association's position in the matter of war contracts were: " Tour committee consider it important, however, in view of certain facts that have been elicited by public inquiry in Ottawa, to offer this statement, so that no stigma can attach to the association for any alleged inaction or indifference."
The report enumerates a number of constructive suggestions which were submitted to the Premier as a practical means of throwing the business "wide open." They were as follows :
1.	That all the requirements of the various departments of the Government, whether for ordinary or special war purposes, should be advertised, and interested manufacturers invited to tender on their supply.
2.	That a permanent Government sample room should be opened at Ottawa, with possibly branch sample-rooms in other points, such as Montreal, Toronto, etc., where, as far as practicable, samples of all goods required would be available for the inspection of contractors.
3.	That in charge of each sample-room there should be an officer to supply inquirers with full particulars as to any kind of Government requirements.
4.	That in the awarding of contracts it should be a standing rule that preference be given in every case, other things being equal, to Canadian products.
5.	That generally speaking, the policy pursued should be frank and open so as to induce Canadian contractors to quote on any lines they might be capable of producing.
The letter concluded with an offer to give free insertion in Industrial Canada to all advertisements calling for tenders from manufacturers, and even to bring out special issues supplementing the regular monthly issue, should such a course be deemed necessary or advisable from the Government's standpoint.
I	do not propose to make any comment on that report. 1 need only say, the facts speak for themselves. Although this correspondence with the 'Canadian Manufacturers' Association has not been brought down, although more than nine months have elapsed since its production was ordered by this House, what has been revealed with regard to it proves conclusively that several duties have been cast upon the Government. In the first place, it is their immediate duty to bring that correspondence down to this House. In the next place, it is their duty to grant a committee of inquiry before which the legitimate manufacturers belonging to that association may appear and justify the warning that they sent to the Prime. Minister in October, 1914. Another duty is incumbent upon them viz-to grant that committee so that these manufacturers may repel the insinuation, as they desire to repel it, that they have in any way been

mixed up in the game of war profiteering. Further, it is the duty of the Government to appoint that committee so that these legitimate manufacturers may make plain who are bona fide manufacturers and who are the mushroom manufacturers that have grown up under the aegis of the Shell Committee and of the Government.
I started on this branch of my subject by stating that there was a general demand for the appointment of a committee of inquiry. The Solicitor General yesterday took exception to the quotations from Liberal newspapers on this subject. Well, I will meet him on that point-in fact, he has already been met on that point. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) read from the Ottawa Evening Journal a demand for that investigation. Now, the significance of that demand lies not so much in the fact that that newspaper is an out-and-out supporter of this Government as in the fact that its editor is a warm personal friend of the Prime Minister. It is not likely that that gentleman would make a demand for an inquiry unless he was very strongly impressed by the absolute necessity fqr investigation. My hon. friend from St. John also read the demand for an investigation from the Montreal Daily Mail in its criticism and ridicule of the valedictory of General Bertram. Again the significance of that demand from the Daily Mail lies not so much in the fact that it also is an out-and-out supporter of this Government as in the fact, that the editor of that paper is a half-brother of the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). So that, with regard to the Daily Mail, we may say that the demand for an investigation comes from within the bosom of the family itself.
The demand has also been made by such staunch Tory papers as the trade journals published by the MacLean Publishing Co., of Toronto, including the Contract Record, the Electrical News, and, I think the Lumberman's Record. In order to satisfy my hon. friend the Solicitor General that I am not quoting from a source friendly to the Liberal party, I will read, first, a declaration of the political faith of the editor of the Electrical News, whose opinion on the subject of investigation I intend to quote. In his issue of the 1st of January, 1916, the editor refers to his criticism of the Government, and says:
Right here at the start let me say that this criticising of the Government is no pleasant task. I am well aware that the publishers of this paper will get little credit for honesty of

purpose. So accustomed is the public to the harpings of the party and corporation press that it has became case-hardened. It has learned to look through the printed articles for the self, party or corporation interest that prompted it. iLet it be known then, once for all, that I prefer the Borden Administration, with all its sins, to a government controlled by a party that sought to tie us up to the United States with a reciprocity treaty. But this paper represents a constituency of business men. It realizes that they are tired of seeing politics practised where business methods should be applied. They know that honest criticism is the best medicine for any government-even if you have to hold its nose while you administer the dose.
We do not propose, anything so drastic as that. The editor goes on:
As I have said before, the publishers are not in a position to handle a war contract and do not care to farm one out.
A little further on in this same article is the following :
We simply want to show that petty politics are no satisfactory substitute, for patriotism, and that party machines cannot do the work of factory lathes.
Surely the Solicitor General could not be supplied with better authority than that. I have gone to a good deal of trouble to get it for him, and I hope he will be satisfied with it. In this same issue of the 1st of January the Electrical News has this further to say on the subject of an investigation :
The public demand an investigation. They look not to the Conservative political machine but to Sir Robert Borden for that investigation. They feel that the Premier who is a gentleman rather than a politician, has been sinned against. They know that when next Sir Robart Borden visits England he will not want to ba pointed out as the sponsor for a committee that scattered its contracts like so much political graft, while our soldiers cried from the trenches for the munitions they so sorely needed. Sir Robert Borden may be deluded by the men he has trusted but he is not the man likely to stand idly by while the good name of the Dominion is dragged through the dirt and grime of a war scandal. Sir Robert Borden will act. Sir Robert Borden must act to save the reputation of the' country he represents and his own political honour.
Further on the same issue the Electrical News discusses this subject of an investigation in this fashion:
The Government has everything to gain and nothing to lose by being open and above-board in the matter. So many stories have been whiskered, so many charges have been flung broadcast that to remain silent must simply be taken as an admission of guilt-an admission that the worst has not been told. Never since Confederation have so many stories of trickery, trafficking and grafting been afloat. They come to this office by the score. All cannot be given because all cannot be investigated.
{Mr. Murphy.]
It would take a big staff working overtime to get into them all. But they pass from mouth to mouth, growing with each telling. Probably most of them have not yet reached Sir Robert Borden. His " machine men " probably see that such as do reach him are fumigated, sugar-coated and otherwise specially prepared for his consumption. But even his own party organs are hinting that makers of munitions " have striven to get large profits out of their contracts." The Toronto News (Conservative) charges it all to " stock market booming," but closes its article with the rather ominous sentences:	" As in previous
crazes a reckoning is coming. It may he close at hand and some very prominent men may be involved in the inevitable disclosures."
That last sentence is quoted by the Electrical News from an editorial in the Toronto Daily News, which, as every one knows, is one of the strongest supporters of this Administration. In view of the opinions of these newspapers which support the Conservative Government of the day, surely it will not be pretended that the demand for investigation is not as strong from the members of the Conservative party as it is from the members of the Liberal party.
The story of how the contracts for the shell boxes were let is also told by the Electrical News in its issue of December 1, 1915. That paper said this:
The purchase of shell boxes was another of the duties of this now famous Shell Committee. Naturally you would expect them to follow the same policy in regard to the boxes. And you won't be disappointed. There was the same secrecy' the same spreading out of contracts to cover commercial or political depression, and the same awarding of contracts to the little fellows regardless of their equipment or financial capacity. That one of the largest box factories in Canada received a contract for 25,000 boxes and manufactured on a sub-contract 50,000 boxes more is eloquent evidence of the business acumen exercised in carrying on this branch of the business. That a Montreal firm not in the box making trade was awarded a contract which it sublet to a box manufacturer in the same city is further evidence that if the committee was honest it was incompetent. That a company of low financial standing was able to secure a large contract, even though it had to construct a new plant for the work, would indicate that the government-for this shell committee stood for the government-had poor relations whose exigencies gave it greater concern than the exigencies of the Empire.
And then, Sir, returning to the subject on January 1, 1916, the Electrical News said:
Just one more instance of how the Shell Committee handled contracts. This story has been investigated and can be vouched for, as can the others that have from time to time found place in this column. The owner of a planing mill in an Ontario town went out after a shell-box contract. His application brought the usual answer that all contracts had been let. Imagine his surprise when a shipping clerk in a dry goods

house in his own town secured a contract, put up a building, completed his contract and got a renewal. The shipping clerk had no plant, no experience and no business rating. But he knew a man who knew something about how contracts were got. Pretty wise man, wasn't he? Thrifty, too. For he still retains Iris job as shipping clerk, though he occasionally finds a few moments to run over to the shell-box plant and figure his profits.
Here is a friend saying to the Government : All the stories that we have published in these columns have been investigated and can be vouched for; grant a committee, and they will be proved before that committee. That, in effect, is what is said by these gentlemen, who prefer the Borden Government, with all their sins, to the Liberal Administration. I ask, Mr. Speaker, how can a Government refuse a friend such a demand as that? Surely the challenge of the Tory editor of the Electrical News will, in any event, not be ignored.
Where is the Electrical News published?

It is one of the publications of the MacLean Publishing Company, of Toronto.
In the course of his speech the hon. member for St. John cited the experience that Mr. F. P. Jones had had with the Shell Committee as a further reason why an investigation should be granted. It seems to me that that incident was so important that the full details of it should be put upon Hansard; it is because I am impressed with a sense of its great importance that I shall venture to do that. The Contract Record, in its issue of November 9, 1915, thus refers to Mr. Jones' experience:
Mr. Jones, like many another, went to Ottawa with a tender for shells. When the contracts were let they went as usual to the favoured few and Mr. Jones was not of them. Those contracts were let at prices^ lower than previous contracts but higher than Mr. Jones' tender. Unlike many another Mr. Jones did not throw up his hands and go home. Instead he went straight to Sir Robert Borden. The Premier was not inclined to listen to a disappointed tenderer, but when Mr. Jones turned to the door with a decisive " Very well, I'll give my statement to the press," he was invited to call again in a couple of days.
Here T interrupt the reading'to say that a little later I shall read a letter written by. Mr. Jones, giving effect to the explanation which the Prime Minister interjected the other day when the hon. member for St. John was referring to the same subject. The article continues:
" On the second visit he found Mr. Thomas with the Premier. Mr. Jones sat down at the
m
typewriter and made three copies of his statement, one for the Premier, one for Mr. Thomas, and the third he kept. That statement showed that the contracts let by the committee were just $21,000,000 higher titan if awarded at the rate of Mr. Jones' tender. A cable to England stopped the contracts before they had been approved by Lloyd George. And in future all contracts for munitions will be open to competitive bids.
"Of course explanations were in order and they were made. It was pointed out that certain concerns had taken risks when shell making was an experiment that might prove costly to the makers and these concerns were entitled to consideration. And probably they were. The [DOT] earlier price charged the Empire was $5.15 for machining a dollar's worth of shell. This was later reduced to $2.90 for doing the same dollar's worth of work. At these figures one would naturally conclude that it was the Empire and not the experimenter, or rather contractor which was entitled to any consideration that was going. Again it was pointed out that policy demanded that the contracts be spread around so as to help relieve commercial depression brought on by the war. And it is only fair to add that this policy has been more or less successful.
There has been no noticeable commercial depression at or near the concern of which Mr. Thomas Cantley is the head and which is said to be making more profits in a month than it ever did before in a year. Neither is the company of which Mr. G. W. Watts is representative making any complaint of hard times. Of course, it is merely a coincidence that Mr. Cantley and Mr. Watts are both members of the Canadian Shell Committee.
It is clearly understood that the manufacturing members of this committee are there in a purely advisory capacity and it is probably to clear them of unjust suspicions that their names are not expected to appear when the new Munitions Committee is appointed.
That article from the Contract Record was widely copied in the Canadian papers. At the request of the right hon. Prime Minister, Mr. Jones wrote a letter explaining what occurred in connection with his interview with the right hon. gentleman. That letter, as reproduced in the Toronto Globe of November 13, 1915, reads as follows:	[DOT]
I called at your house by appointment in regard to the manufacture of shells. After hearing what I had to say you informed me that I should place my representations before Mr. D. A. Thomas, who was acting for the British Government, and who was then in Canada. To this I agreed, and accordingly you then consulted by telephone with Mr. Thomas, who was then in Montreal, and arranged that I should interview him for that purpose in the immediate future. The interview as arranged took place within forty-eight hours. I never saw you and Mr. Thomas together, and I never said or in any way intimated that I would give any statement to the press, nor had I any intention of doing so. The statement which has appeared in the press with regard to my interview with you is utterly unfounded. You received me most courteously, and listened attentively to everything I had to say, after which the interview was arranged as above stated with Mr. Thomas.

That letter, Mr. Speaker, is all very well so far as it goes; but, as you will not have failed to notice, it leaves the serious charges quite untouched. For instance, it says nothing about the prices previously allowed to manufacturers by the Shell Committee being very considerably higher than the prices at which Mr. Jones was prepared to make the same class of shells. It also leaves untouched the published statement of the Contract Record that Mr. Jones had shown the Premier that a saving of $21,000,000 could have been effected on the previous shell orders had the Shell Committee awarded them at the rate of Mr. Jones' tender.
It further leaves untouched the other statement that the contracts already let at t'he higher figure and sent to Mr. Lloyd George for approval had been stopped by cable. These rather important details being overlooked in Mr. Jones' letter, you will not be surprised that the letter did not satisfy the Contract Record. An editorial from that paper on the subject of Mr. Jones' letter was reproduced in the Ottawa Citizen of November 26, 1915, and is in these terms.-
At the request of Sir Robert Borden, Mr. F. P. Jones, of the Canada Cement Corporation, has oome forward with a sort of blanket denial of the story of his interview with the Premier re the shell game. According to . Mr. Jones' statement, Mr. Thomas was not present at that interview, nor did he threaten to make a statement to the press if his tenders were not given proper consideration. He admits, however, that Sir Robert sent him to Mr. Thomas, and 'to ensure him due consideration in that quarter, called up Lloyd George's representative and an anged the interview. Mr. Jones further states that at the interview arranged by the Premier, Mr. Thomas warned him that tenders would be called for.
It would appear from the above that Mr. Jones is not taking the public entirely into his confidence. He neglects to mention why it was necessary to call on the Premier and later attend a premier-arranged interview with Mr. Thomas in order to acquire the valuable information that tenders for shells would be called for.
He also neglects to mention whether he had first been to the shell committee with his proposition. Of course, if he had, it might be necessary to go to either Sir Robert Borden or Mr. Thomas in search of such valuable infor-' mation as he received. Were not the shell committee representing Canada in regard to the purchase of shells? Were they not giving out information in regard to the asking for tenders? Were they not using their every endeavour and undoubted business ability to secure for the Empire the munitions she needed and in the cheapest market? Apparently not, for Mr. Jones, according to his own statement, had to go first to the Premier and then to Mr. Thomas before he could discover that tenders we e to be. asked for. But please note the
[Mr. Murphy. J
grateful sequel:	" Our company again tendered and I am pleased to say got business at the prices tendered by us." These little words 41 again tendered " are an indication that previous to his interviews with Sir Robert Borden and Mr. Thomas, his company had been in the field for shell contracts. Why doesn't Mr. Jones go further and tell the public why his other tenders had been turned down, and why he found it necessary to go over the heads of the shell committee before his tenders received the consideration they merited and his factories the orders subsequent events show they were entitled to?
Blanket denials are not explanations, and it is explanations that are in order at the present time. Mr. Thomas has stated that i>rofits of the manufacturers have been higher than they were entitled to ; the shell committee has been allowed to drift into oblivion, and evidently requested to do its drifting with the least possible noise; it has been replaced by a Munitions Committee, which is in the hands, and evidently under the complete control of Mr. Lionel Hichens, who has come out from England as the personal representative of Mr. Lloyd George. What does this all mean? Why, if the story told here is ndt true, was the shell committee abolished?
This column admitted on the start that it was impossible to get sworn statements. It is so still. Consequently, it is impossible to be exact as to details. But the essentials of the story of the breaking up of the shell game have yet to be denied. The interviews be* tween Mr. Jones, Sir Robert Borden, and Mr. Thomas took place. They were followed by the disappearance of the shell committee. A report was senj: out from Ottawa that all munition contracts had been cancelled. A competitive system of tendering replaced the old haphazard system. And big firms got contracts who had not been able to get even information concerning them before.
Just why it is impossible to get exact details is perhaps shown by several letters addressed to this column. They come from contract holders in Toronto, and, in each case the writer complains that his firm cannot get any more contracts because it is accused of giving things away.
As you are aware, this Government appointed what is colloquially referred to as' the War Purchasing Committee. That committee, I understand, is under the chairmanship of the member of the Government without portfolio, the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp). Public attention was directed to that committee by a charge published in a Toronto paper called Men's Wear, to the effect that a clothing contract had been awarded to a Toronto real estate agent, one Carl F. Hopkins. In course of time that charge was taken up by the Davidson Commission, and, not to trouble the House with too many details, it was found by that Commission that the particular contract referred to in Men's Wear was a contract for clothing for the British Government, and therefore did not come within the scope of the Commission. But, in the

course of the inquiry it was revealed that this Toronto real estate dealer, Mr. Carl F. Hopkins, had, as the Empire Clothing Company,, got another contract, and this other contract he obtained from the Militia Department of this Government. Some of the facts brought out with reference to that Militia Department contract before the Davidson Commission are illuminating. In the Toronto Globe of December 30, 1915, I find this report of the proceedings of the day previous at the sitting of the Davidson Commission in Ottawa:
Ottawa, December 29.-The " Men's Wear " charges as to the granting of Canadian military clothing contracts were again before the Davidson War Contracts Commission this morning.
Mr. J. V. Reid, secretary of the Contracts Branch of the Militia Department, was the first witness. He produced a letter written on March 29 last by C. F. Hopkins of Toronto, to the Director of Contracts, stating that it was immaterial whether a contract was given to C. F. Hopkins and Company or the Empire Clothing Company-whose name was on the patronage list-so long as one was secured. A contract was actually given in August to the Empire Clothing Company for 12,000 pairs of trousers, being secured by tender. Hopkins himself had received no contract.
The letter referred to, which was produced from the files of the Militia Department, was headed:
" C. F. Hopkins & Co., clothing manufacturers, factories 150-160 John street, office 30 Adelaide street, Toronto; cable address; Hoco." The letter was addressed to P. W. Brown, director of contracts, Militia Department, Ottawa, and was as follows:
" Dear Sir,-Following my phone conversation with you this afternoon, I sent you views showing some of the interior of our plant and also a letter from one of my partners which will explain itself.
" It does not matter whether we receive the orders for clothing in the name of the Empire Clothing Co or of C F Hopkins and Co., clothing manufacturers, so long as we receive them.
" According to your letter of December 18, 1914, our name has been on the patronage list for the supply of clothing since that date. We have received no word or contract, although several of the members have spoken on our behalf.
" Since I spoke to you last, I understand that the clothing for the third contingent has practically all been ordered, and I trust we may secure a portion of the next clothing order."
It, is peculiar that, in this investigation before the Davidson Commission, this Toronto real estate clothing dealer, Mr. Hopkins, was not called as a witness.
Mr. Acton, the man responsible for the publication of the article in Men's Wear, was called as a witness, and if one can judge by newspaper reports of the proceedings, he was dealt with rather severely by the commissioner. In point of fact, he was handled in such a fashion that you would think that he, and not Hopkins, was the
guilty party. Eventually he was induced to hand in a sort of half apology for having dared to make the statements that he had made in Men's Wear. Now, these somewhat peculiar happenings before the Davidson Commission led the editor of the Electrical News-you remember him, Mr. Speaker, the gentleman who said that with all its sins he preferred the Borden Government to the Liberal administration-in the issue of January 15, 1916, to say this:
We are informed from Ottawa that the work of the Davidson investigation commission is almost finished. To criticise that work would probably be considered contempt of court and I would hate to be the only one to receive punishment at its hands. But I fain would ask a question or two. Surely one may venture that far. And my first query would naturally be: "In the Hopkins investigation was it Mr. Hopkins or Mr. Acton who was being investigated?" And following this would it be unwise or unkindly to ask why Mr. Hopkins was not called to the stand? Mr. Hopkins' home is in Toronto, but he is taking most of his meals at the Biltmore Hotel in New York city. I believe he prefers the New York climate and if he does spend an occasional Sunday in Toronto it is because his family still resides in the Queen city. Of course he might have gone to Ottawa as a witness but those attorneys have a way of talking to mere witnesses that does not make their position* in the box an attractive one.
Further light on the work of this Davidson Commission is thrown by an editorial of the Toronto Globe of December 15, 1915, in which the editor of that paper discusses the distribution of an order for 188,000 pairs of trousers. I will read a few paragraphs from the editorial in question:
The only cure for the suspicion that army contracts are being awarded by favour at excessive prices is publicity. When the names of successuful tenderers, the prices quoted by them, and the quantity of goods ordered from them are published in the Press unsuccessful bidders can at once learn why they did not obtain the order or a share of it. In the case of the trousers contract, whidh is the subject of judicial inquiry, the commission did not award the contract to the lowest tenderer, 5 p.m. but split it up among a considerable number of bidders, all of whom were paid the price at which they tendered. This, Mr. Kemp explains, was done because there was urgent need for the clothing and because there would inevitably have been delay had the lowest tenderer been given the entire contract. An order for 188,000 pairs of trousers was distributed among ten eastern Canadian firms and several in the west, the units averaging about 12,500 pairs. The eastern companies participating and the prices per pair at which they tendered and at which each company did the work were as follows:
Price per pair.
T. Eaton Co., Toronto	$320
A. Kilbert & Co., Montreal	 3 28
Crown Pants Co., Montreal	 3 43
Copley, Noyes & Randall, Hamilton. 3 43

Price per pair.
Cohen & Sons, Montreal	$3 50
Punchard, Burril & Co., Toronto ..	3 58
Canada Clothing Co., Montreal....	3 64
Empire Clothing Co., Toronto. .	. .	3 69
W. E. Sanford Mfg. Co., Hamilton. 3 72
Capital Brand Trousers, Toronto ..	3 73
Had the contract gone to the lowest tenderer -the T. Eaton Co.-the total cost to the country would have been exactly $40,000 less than it was under the system of " divvying up " and giving each firm the price it asked for. Was the need for haste served by this extra price? It is stated by Mr. Kemp that the Eaton Co. had half a million dollars' worth of government work on hand when the trousers contract was awarded. Was that work of such a nature as to stand in the way of the speedy carrying out of the trousers contract? Had the "Capital Brand " company, for example- which is unknown to the most important houses in the clothing trade in this city, and which got $6,625 more for making 12,500 pairs of trousers than the Eaton Co. would have charged for the same work-greater facilities for turning out this clothing in a hurry than the Eaton Co.?
Would you have liked them to go without trousers?

I must ask my hon. friend the Minister of Customs to solve his own conundrums. My hon. friend the Solicitor General quoted from an article which had appeared in the Toronto' Globe in approval of the Davidson commission. May I be permitted to say that that article was written prior to the hearing of this case by the Davidson Commission, and that after that case was heard the Globe was not exactly of the same opinion. Here is what the Globe said after the Men's Wear charges had been gone into:
Is Mr. Kemp playing politics with army orders instead of awarding them to the lowest tenderer irrespective of politics as Sir Robert Borden promised? It looks very much like it. That apology of Brother Acton was distinctly premature. The Public Accounts Committee of the House of Commons should spend an hour or two in the company of Mr. Carl F. Hopkins real estate dealer in the main and clothing manufacturer on the side and learn who the members were who spoke " on our behalf " before the Kemp Purchasing Commission was appointed and whose influence was so potent that after the .commission took charge the Empire Clothing Co. was given 49 cents per pair more fq_r making army trousers than the lowest tenderer.
There is nothing said against the commissioner in that Globe article.

No, there is nothing said against him, but may I point out to the Solicitor General, that there is nothing said in his favour? Of the methods pursued by this War Purchasing Committee the Electrical News offers pointed criticism.

In its issue of December 1 last, after referring to the fact that this War Purchasing Committee was staggering along under a sharp fusilade of criticism, it stated:
But here again that scattering of contracts to cover that same commercial depression creeps in and brings forth the usual criticism. The segregation of tenders thus rendered necessary often practically wipes out competition and the net result is that the big concerns are often neglected while may a sweat shop with a machine hastily stuck in a cellar is working night and day to turn out materials that do not keep the equipment up to the requirements of enlistment. Some of the big concerns are prepared to take this work at actual cost in order to keep their factories running and their staffs together. But the system in vogue does not give them a chance.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in view of these disclosures, taken from responsible public journals in this country, I submit that the public will not be satisfied unless the work of this War Purchasing Committee is included in the scope of whatever investigating committee may be appointed by Parliament to go into the subject of war contracts generally.
You recall, Mr. Speaker, that throughout a large part of last session a special committee of this House sat to investigate the contracts that were awarded 'by the Militia Department for boots and shoes. You will further recall that, in connection with that investigation, it was disclosed that in one case a middleman had received over $15,000 for securing contracts for an old and well-known boot and shoe manufacturing concern in the city of Quebec. You would naturally have expected, Mr. Speaker, that, in view of the disclosures before that special committee of this House, war graft in boots, in any event, would have stopped. Well, Sir, I am sorry to inform you that it has not. I have under my hand a copy of the court record of a suit entered in the Superior Court in the City of Quebec. The plaintiff is a gentleman of the name of Frank W. Belmer. The defendant is the John Ritchie Company, a long-established and highly respected firm in the city of Quebec. The plaintiff, Belmer, produced a contract in writing whereby he was appointed to act as middleman between the John Ritchie Company and the Government for the purpose of securing contracts for boots and contracts for canvas shoes.
Who were the parties to the contract?

The contract is contained in two letters, dated respectively

October 13 and October 28, 1914, signed by Mr. Warrington, secretary of the John Ritchie Company, and addressed to Frank W. Relmer, Quebec. Belmer alleges that under this written contract he secured orders for boots and shoes for the John Ritchie Company from the Militia Department. The contract stipulates that Belmer is to be paid a commission of fifty cents a pair on every contract for boots he secures for the John Ritchie Company from the Militia Department, and a commission of thirty cents a pair on every pair .of canvas shoes. It is not alleged in court that Belmer makes any claim for any commission in connection with the boot contract, but apart from the record I am informed that lie was paid a very considerable sum of money for the boot contracts he obtained. Belmer claims, and in fact this constitutes his whole claim, that through his agency the John Ritchie Company o'b-tained from the Department of Militia and Defence between October, 1914, and November, 1915, contracts for 150,000 pairs of canvas shoes, and he accordingly claims the sum of $45,000 commission, which is at the rate of thirty cents a pair on the 150,000 pairs. It is only fair to say that the defendant company does not admit that the plaintiff is entitled to any commission with respect to the canvas shoes. But the written contract-and this is tne most immoral part of the whole proceeding-this written contract by which Belmer is appointed as middleman or go-between for the John Ritchie Company the defendants do not dispute. Surely, Mr. Speaker, if ever there was a case that ought to be investigated, this case of Bel-mer is the one.
Hear, hear.
What was the result of the action?
It has not been tried yet. The defendant .disputes the plaintiff's claim, and the action is still in court.
It could be investigated by the Public Accounts Committee.
Parliament is the High Court of the nation, and any investigation that is held should be held under the direc- [DOT] tion of Parliament.
I said it could he investigated by the Public Accounts Committee.

Certainly. I was proceeding to say that instances could be multiplied of middlemen acting in other
capacities, with a loss to the Government in each case; but I have already taken up a great deal of the time of the House, and I feel it would be loading up Hansard unnecessarily if I were to enumerate these cases. I submit that I have made it clear that a demand for an investigation is general on the part of the public, and the necessity for it is such that without it the honour of this Government, the honour of this Parliament, and the honour of this country, can never be vindicated.
Let me now refer somewhat briefly to the speech made by my hon. friend the Solicitor General yesterday. Considered in the large, that speech may be divided into two parts; that part in which he laboured to prove that his colleague the Minister of Finance, did not say what he meant, or did not mean what he said, when he answered the inquiry of the hon. member for St. John as to whether this Government was paying the whole cost of the Canadian overseas expeditionary forces, and that part in. which he laboured an attack against the hon. member for St. John, and sought to minimize the effect of that hon. gentleman's speech by showing that here and there he had been mistaken as to a name, or a date, or a place, as, for instance, when he said that the Solicitor General had delivered a speech at Fort William when it should have been Portage la Prairie. The hon. member for St. John exposed this afternoon some of these mental acrobatics on the part of the Solicitor General, and' it is therefore unnecessary for me to Tefer to these particular things. I have just this to say, that, listening as I did yesterday, and as I always do, with great interest to what the Solicitor General had to say, I was more than ever impressed with the strikingly strong resemblance between the hon. gentleman and the famous knight, Sir Hudihras, immortalized by Butler. Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, Sir Hudibras as Butler depicted him? Perhaps you have forgotten, so for your benefit and the benefit of the House I will just quote his description:
He was in logic a great critic Profoundly skilled in analytic;
He could distinguish and divide A hair 'twixt south and southwest side; On either which he would dispute, Confute, change hands, and ' still confute.
That is a perfect picture of the Solicitor General, and the resemblance between him and the worthy knight was never so striking as it was yesterday. He laboured long and valiantly to extricate his col-

league the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) from the difficulty into which it was evident he feared the Minister of Finance had got by the answers he made to the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) on Tuesday last. It was somewhat amusing to us on this side of the House to see the agitation that broke out on the benches opposite immediately after the Minister of Finance had made those answers to the hon. member for St. John. The Minister of Finance himself was obviously disturbed. He moved uneasily in his seat; he moved out of his seat; be went around the opposite side of the House talking to his friends; he was obviously ill at ease. Now, why should he be ill at ease, and why should the Solicitor General labour to prove that his words did not mean exactly what he said and what he intended them to mean? The Minister of Finance was asked an ordinary and a proper question. Like an honest man he gave that question an honest answer. Yesterday my hon. friend the member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) emphasized the honesty and the point of that answer. The matter has evidently become one of such agitation in Government circles that I propose to put upon Hansard again question and answer as they fell from the lips of the two hon. gentlemen on Monday last. On page 42 of Hansard I find the following, referring to the previous answer given by the Minister of Finance:
Mr. Pugsley: That means, of course, all the ammunition, all the guns, all the boots and shoes, and all the clothing used by the Canadian soldiers at the front?
Sir Thomas White: Our understanding is that the Canadian Government will pay all, but that an adjustment is necessary and will have to take .place later.
Mr. F. W. Maclean: Does that include transportation?
Sir Thomas White: I speak subject to correction by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, but I believe that the Canadian Government has agreed to pay all the cost of transportation also; in other words, we desire to pay the entire cost of the Canadian Expeditionary Force abroad.
It cannot have been many minutes aftei the Minister of Finance had made that perfectly honest and frank statement that somebody whispered in his ear:	" Why,
you have, given the whole case away; when you admit that we are paying for tnese things, then we cannot dispute the right of Parliament to investigate them." That explains the disturbance on the opposite side of the House. Now, I submit that my hon. friend the Solicitor General did not make the matter any better by his hand-

ling of it yesterday. He spent a good deal of his time in an attack upon the hon. member for St. John; but as part of that attack was lepelled by that hon. member this afternoon, it is unnecessary for me to refer to it at any length.
I want, however, to refer to one matter in regard to which the Solicitor General waxed warm and indignant. He accused the hon. member for St. John of misrepresenting what he, the Solicitor General, had said in a speech at Portage la Prairie about taxing war profits.
