And doubtless he will make good his accusations by some such formal step before the session is very much older.
In any case, the Government cannot permit these shocking and humiliating charges to remain uninvestigated. We are confident that no Canadian Government will hide behind the technicality that the money, said to be worse than wasted, was British money, entrusted to us to he carefully spent amidst the strain of a great

war, and not our own money. That would he to confess and proclaim that we would be less honest in dealing with sacred trust funds than in handling our personal property.
If a pound of British money, entrusted to a Canadian committee to buy the greatest possible amount of war material, was allowed to be diverted to Canadian private purses in inordinate profits, then the men guilty of this sordid and despicable treason were guilty of weakening by just so much the fighting forces of the Empire in the face of an appalling peril. They might as well have gone to the trenches and taken the rifles out of the hands of our boys, fronting a German attack, and then sold these rifles for their personal profit to the first second-hand dealer whom they met. If this has been done, the country wants to know it, regardless of legal technicalities or partisan politics.
A thorough investigation into this whole shell game should be set on foot at once.
In contrast with the sordid greed of the war profiteers, and to show the brighter side of human nature, I want to pay a tribute, before I conclude, to an American gentleman resident in Philadelphia, who has set an example that we may well follow. The name of this gentleman is Albert C. Middleton. He was virtually the proprietor of the Victor Talking Machine Company, in conducting the business of which he made several millions of dollars; now, though under fifty years of age, he is practically retired from business. His American company had an English connection, the 'Gramaphone 'Company, of England. This English company lias a large contract for supplying war munitions. One of the [DOT] managers of the English company requested this Philadelphia gentleman to purchase munitions in the United States. Mr. Middleton agreed. Up to May last he had sent to England about $30,000,000 worth of munitions, and he had placed orders in the United States for as many millions more. The bills for all these munitions were sent to this American gentleman of high repute, and were paid on his personal voucher. For doing all this, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Middleton not only made no charge, but he actually paid the expenses of the office staff necessary to look after these war munition orders. And, Sir, when he was asked why he gave gratuitously the services of 'himself and his staff, the only reply that he made was: "I am deeply interested in the Allies' cause." I think that I would be correctly interpreting the feeling of this House and of the people of Canada if I should thank that man in the name of the people of this Dominion for the unselfish service that he has rendered gratuitously to the cause in which we are all so deeply
interested. I am satisfied that there are many men in Canada who would do as Mr. Middleton has done if they were but given the chance, and I appeal to my hon. friends in the Government to give every man who is willing to bear a man's part in this great struggle the chance to play his part.
One word more in conclusion, and by way of pointing the moral that I want to bring home to the members of this Government. There has been laid before you, Sir, a portion only of the black record of the . war profiteers. But even that portion is so bad that, not unnaturally, you ask yourself:	by what process of
reasoning could these men justify what they have done? Let me, Sir, suggest an answer to that question. If the war profiteers reasoned at all, it occurs to me that they must have followed a course of reasoning similar to that which, it is said, a former generation of medical men used to employ in dealing with certain desperate cases. You are aware, Sir, that in the crisis of a serious malady the bleeding of a patient was often said to turn the scale towards healthy life. Possibly with that in mind, and, in any event, looking at Canada in the crisis of this war, the profiteers must have reasoned thus: as with individuals, so with nations, so even with empires; therefore, at this critical stage in Canada's life, financial phlebotomy on a national scale has become necessary as a desperate remedy. And to work they went, with knife and tomahawk, all the time loudly proclaiming:
True patriots we; for, be it understood,
We bleed our country for our country's good.
Mr. Speaker, the first and paramount duty of this Parliament is to provide a ligature that will stop the country's bleeding. That ligature can take only the form of an investigating committee, and, as one of the representatives of the people of this country, I now ask this Government to appoint such a committee without one moment's further delay.

The hon. gentleman raised the question as to what was the true meaning of the visit of the Prime Minister of Canada to the councils of the Empire. I confess that I am unable at this time to give an answer to that question; I do not know what the answer will in the course of time be. Twenty years ago the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, speaking on the subject of imperial federation, said that he was almost afraid to speak on that subject for fear he might lose his reputation as a practical statesman. He said, too, that imperial federation was described by many as a dream, but that somehow or other, it was one of those dreams that seemed to fasten themselves upon the public imagination, and dreams that impress the public in that way somehow or other had a way of coming true. Our Empire has travelled far since Mr. Joseph Chamberlain gave expression to that opinion. At the time of the South African war, owing to the part played by the people of Canada, the relations which existed between the Motherland and the colonies were vastly changed. I do not know what may be the true significance of the visit of the Canadian Premier to the councils of the Empire, but I do know that when it was cabled to Canada and to the different parts of the Empire throughout the world it kindled fires of Imperial patriotism that, when we associate with it the great sacrifices of treasure and blood that have been made by the colonies in this great struggle, will, it seems to me, have a tremendous influence on the future development of the Empire. We may not know at the present time what may be the future position of the colonies and their relation to the iMotiherllanid but we do know that never again will the people of this Empire be satisfied with the relations that have existed in the past.

This man was associated with a company located in Quebec called the Gauthier Company, which was at that time conducted by the widow of the man Gauthier, who founded it. She had assumed that business, and was carrying it on as a limited liability company. There was associated with her as a commercial traveller a man named Charles Slater. He had been in the past, owing to his experience in the shoe business, as was brought out in the investigation, the shoe expert of the late Government. That shows the estimation in which they held his ability. This man represented to this lady, who was conducting this business, that, through the influence which tin possessed with the Government at Ottawa, if she would pay him a commission of 5 per cent, on any orders which she might receive from the Government, he would use his influence in getting those orders. What are the facts? The Gauthier Company, in common with many other shoe manufacturing concerns throughout the Dominion of Canada, were awarded contracts for shoes. They filled those contracts. They received their contract at exactly the same price as was paid to other manufacturers. This man represented to this woman that it was through his own influence that he had secured this order.
I submit that an arrangement of that kind, entered into in that way, in so far as this Government or any other Government might be concerned, involved nothing discreditable or disreputable. I may say further that this same firm, owing to just such careless, such unbusinesslike methods, have since gone into insolvency, very largely as the result of their operations in these war contracts, and have been able to pay their creditors only a small percentage of their liabilities.	,

It does not seem to me a matter for wonder, however, that there has been a continued decrease in imports from Great Britain to Canada. I think that decrease can be attributed to other reasons than the tariff. For instance, the importation of steel from Great Britain to Canada has decreased. Steel is a very important industry in Great Britain, but at the present time Great Britain is so absorbed in carrying on the war, and her industries are so much engaged in turning out munitions, that she has no steel to spare for Canada and the other countries of the world. The same thing applies to woollens. The woollen mills of Canada are busier at the present time, perhaps, than they have ever been before. This is one of the cases cited as showing that there has been wrongdoing in the letting of shell contracts. It seems to me that if something of a more substantial nature than this cannot be charged against the Shell Committee, there surely is not at the present time any gropnd for an investigation.
There have been other rumours. Last night there was brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) something that went further than, mere rumour, a quotation from* the columns of a New York financial paper. It referred to a letter written by Sir Henry M. Pellatt, president of the Steel and Radiation Company of Canada, naming prices being paid for certain classes of shells in Canada. I do not wish to take up the time of the House by going over this entire lartidle. In effect, the situation is this: Sir Henry Pellatt writes to New York financial interests that the company of which he is the president had received contracts for the manufacture of shells, and that on this first contract his profit is going to be $250,000, and that he has another contract that will show a profit of $200,000. Now,
I submit to the judgment of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House that if they were legitimate manufacturers engaged in the production of shells and had their own business to carry on, would it be reasonable to suppose that they would write a letter of that kind giving to the public the profit they were going to make. Who is Sir Henry Pellatt? Is he a great captain of industry? I have never heard him so described. He is a member of the firm of Pellatt & Pellatt, stockbrokers, of the city of Toronto. Sir Henry Pellatt, when he

wrote that letter, wrote it as one form of advertising. He is not concerned about the profits that are going to be made out of the shell industry in Canada. He is playing for bigger game. He wants the impression to go abroad in Wall street, in the stock exchanges of Toronto and Montreal, that he is getting big, fat, round contracts for war munitions, and he has got a war stock that he is going to sell to the unsuspecting public.
X come from a place where shells are being manufactured as successfully as in any part of this Dominion of Canada- and the work is carried on not -Jor stooK-jobbing purposes, but as a legitimate manufacturing enterprise. In connection with the shell orders that have been given in my constituency-and many have been given up to the present time-I may say that 75 per cent of the profits are represented to-day in the capital cost of new machinery and equipment. I know nothing of the operations of the stock market, but I will guarantee that Steel and Radiation stock, simultaneously with the announcement to which I haye referred, was placed upon the market in the stock exchanges of Canada and the United States. I will guarantee also that that stock had a phenomenal rise, and that when this war is over, Sir Henry Pellatt will not hold that stock and will not be in a position to receive those war dividends-the unsuspecting public will once again have been taken in. I believe that the case of the Steel and Radiation Company may be taken as a fair sample of where this agitation has come from with regard to the abnormal profits that are being made in the production of shells.
I do not wish to enter into any discussion as to what might have happened if hon. gentlemen opposite had held the reins of power in August, 1914. I myself am persuaded that if Sir Wilfrid Lauriei had been Prime Minister of this country at the time war broke out, he would have given to the service of 'his country all the earnestness and zeal that patriotic enthusiasm could command. But I desire to say that the people of Canada have followed the record of the Borden Administration since the war began. They have observed the way in which the Prime Minister of this country has assumed and discharged the duties of that difficult position; the way in which the Minister of Militia has fulfilled his arduous task; the way in which the Minister of Finance has guided our financial course during a
most difficult and trying period; the way in which the other members of the Cabinet have measured up to the situation. And I may add-when all this passion that is being aroused has passed away, hon. gentlemen will agree with me-that I would include the Shell Committee amongst those who have given magnificent service to their country. When I think of what the 'Government has done during these trying times; when I think of the way in which they have represented the genius and the aspirations of the Canadian people, as a humble member of the party which I represent, I am indeed proud.
I feel that I must not too long transgress upon the time of this House. As I said before, I have taken a great deal of pleasure in listening to the speeches that have been delivered in this debate, and I think that the tone of them has been splendid, and creditable indeed to this House of Commons. I am not one of those who think that the Opposition should sit still and say nothing. I think that if there is anything, even in the present situation, that demands criticism, hon. gentlemen opposite would be derelict in their duty if they hesitated to criticise it. But it seems to me that when we think of what has been accomplished in this country, when we think of what the country has passed through, and of the opportunities that there have been for irregularities-, when we consider that nothing more substantial has been brought against the record of this Administration, our affairs have indeed been conducted in an honourable and creditable manner.
Reference has been made to certain agitators in the province of Quebec, of whom we as Canadian people do not feel proud. In this respect I am prepared to gncept the view of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), who said the other day that we must look not to the Bourassas and the Lavergnes for an expression of the feelings and sentiments of the French-Canadian people, but that we may find those sentiments properly expressed in the speeches that have been delivered by the Lauriers and the Casgrains. I believe implicitly that that is a proper summing-up of the situation. In regard to the statements that have been made recently in the Quebec legislature, I believe such is the benign influence of British institutions, that these men will live to regret the day that they ever gave expression to such sentiments, and that their children, whatever thffir fathers may



have advocated, will be loyal and patriotic Canadians.
As I endeavoured to catch the spririt underlying the opinions of hon. gentlemen of this House, and as I tried to think of what I might appropriately say on this occasion, it seemed to me that in concluding the remarks that I was to make to-night, I could not do better than quote to the House an extract from a spech delivered more than fifty years ago by a distinguished member of Parliament. .He was speaking for unity; for the removal of race and class prejudices. The late Thomas D'Arcy McGee, in the course of an address in which he was speaking of the future of Canada-and with these words I shall conclude-said:
All we have to do is, each for himself, to keep down dissensions which can only weaken, impoverish, and keep hack the country; each for himself, to do all he can to increase its wealth, its strength, and its reputation; each for himself-you and you, gentlemen, and all of us-to welcome every talent, to hail every invention, to cherish every gem of art, to foster every gleam of authorship, to honour every acquirement and every natural gift; to lift ourselves to the level of our destinies, to rise above all low limitations and narrow conscriptions ; to cultivate that true catholicity of spirit which embraces all creeds, all classes and all races in order to make of our boundless Canada, so rich in known and unknown resources, a great new northern nation.

Mr. Speaker, before I enter upon the subject of my remarks on this occasion, I deem it my duty to offer you my congratulations on your elevation to the seat which you now occupy, knowing that in that [DOT]position you will display the dignity which you have shown in an inferior seat, and that impartiality will at all times characterize your actions, as we have seen even during the few days you have presided over this House.
I have listened with great attention to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the Throne. It has been my pleasure in other sessions to listen with gratification and admiration to the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Alfred Thompson). On this occasion he has again been equal to the task imposed on him, and his speech will remain among the cherished records of Canada for many years to come. The seconder of the address has recalled to this House many of. the deeds of the French Canadian people from the province of Quebec in the present war. I need not mention the speeches of the right hon. Prime Minister and the right hon.
fMr. Scott.]
leader of the Opposition, who have both been equal to the task of the day. It was my pleasure again to listen to the eloquent
address of the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain), who also reminded this Parliament and the country of the deeds which have been acomplished in the field of battle by French Canadians from the province of Quebec. He gave us some information as to the number of soldiers who have gone to the front from that province, many of whom have already come back with glory, while others have given their lives and died the death of heroes, in defence of the sacred cause of liberty, -justice and right. I join with these gentlemen in paying honour to the members of the French-Canadian race from the province of Quebec and from Western Canada for the part they have taken in this great war. ~
But I rise to say that far to the east of Quebec,' along the coast of the Atlantic and the gulf of iSt. Lawrence, there is also an element of the French race, in the land of Evangeline, the forest primeval so poetically described by Longfellow, now converted into prosperous towns and villages, and happy homes, blessed with large families, educated to the forgiveness of the harshness of conquest in the present enjoyment of the glorious faculties of British citizenship, the Acadians of the Maritime provinces, who, in this present crisis, have given testimony of their love of country and their appreciation of the benefits of British citizenship equal to that given by any other section of the Canadian people. As senior member for the Acadian people in this House, representing the largest number of Acadian'S in the Maritime Provinces, who opened to me the gate of this sanctuary some sixteen years ago and have kept it open for me on. every occasion since that time, I deem it my duty to make you acquainted with what has been- going on among the Acadian people in the Maritime Provinces. Let me tell you that the efforts of the French race in the province of Quebec have been equalled -I say it with pride-by those of the Maritime Provinces. Not only the common citizens among the Acadians have given their attention to the position in which Canada has been placed through this turmoil of European war, but every man of intelligence of every position, every Acadian pHest in the Maritime Provinces, has devoted his time, his efforts, his eloquence, to calling upon the young men of his place to enlist with others and go and

defend their country by defending the rule of Britannia. It h>as been my pleasure on many occasions during the last year to address recruiting meetings in my county. There is not one district which I have not visited, and in many of them, especially in the larger places such as Bathurst, where the population is mixed, we have always had the ministers of the nonCatholic denominations side by side; with the Catholic priest; and in every other district, the French districts more particularly, every meeting was presided oveT by the parish priest; and as my hon. friend Mr. Lemieux said of the Province of Quebec, in any place where no hall or schoolhouse afforded sufficient accommodation for the multitude, the vestry of the church of the locality was open to the recruiting meetings, presided over, as I say, by the parish priest.
The hon. the Postmaster General, as well as the seconder of the Address, in order to ishow to the country at large, as welll as to this House, the unanimity of action of the whole people, more particularly among the ecclesiastical authorities, has read to this House the noble words that have fallen from the lips of the Archbishop of Quebec and the Archbishop of Montreal.
I am sure that every one in this House will be edified by his words, and that they will be read by future generations, Will you permit me, Mr. Speaker, to read a few more passages to the House. I am sure you will agree that no more patriotic, no more eloquent and fervid appeal has been made during the war than that made by the only Acadian Bishop in the Maritime Provinces, Bishop Leblanc, of St. John, at a public meeting held in the city of iSt. John on the 1st November, 1014. This is what he said:
As Canadians our cause is bound up with the cause of Britain her interests are ours; if England falls we are going to fall with her, and we are going to lose all the glorious privileges we enjoy as citizens of the British Empire. Canada now so free and so happy, so blessed by God with such great resources, Canada that has such a brilliant future before her, will be reduced to a condition of vassalage and crushed under the iron heel of a foreign 'and unsympathetic ruler.
Failure for England in this war will mean England's destruction and even success will have to be dearly paid for; but, let us thank God, the age of chivalry is not passed; there is still enough patriotism and heroism in the young men of this province to make a supreme effort now for England's cause. Our hope is in our young men, to them we look to uphold the honour and the glory of the British Empire,
of that empire which, rather than break its plighted word to gallant little Belgium, has been willing to sacrifice the best and noblest of her sons
Coming from such a high dignitary, these words could not fail to have a beneficent effect, and I may say that since then, on more than one occasion, Bishop Leblanc has given expression to similar sentiments at French gatherings, more particularly at Moncton and Shediac. May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that a great number of Aca-dians have enlisted in the military forces. They have enlisted in every county of the Maritime Provinces. I know whereof I speak, so far 'as the counties of New Brunswick are concerned, and I think the hon. members from Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, who represent consituenoies containing French elements, can testify to the fact that in their constitu-9 p.m. encies also the Acadian peqple have risen to the occasion. Hundreds and thousands of them have already gone to the front, and only recently, just before the Christmas holidays, it was decided to form an Acadian, battalion.
I desire' to extend to my hon. friend the Minister of Militia my congratulations upon his prompt response to the request of the Acadian people. At present they are engaged throughout the counties of New Brunswick and other parts of the Maritime Provinces in forming a battalion of their own, with their own officers, and, let me add, with their own chaplain. Only a few days ago, just as I was about to leave my home to come here to attend to my duties in Parliament, we received a report in Bathurst that two brave young men from the county of Gloucester had been killed in action. One, Cyril Vigot, though born on the island of Jersey, had been a resident at Caraquet, in the county of Gloucester for many years. He bad left one of the best positions open to young men in the county of Gloucester, having been manager of one of the branches of the Loggie Company in Caraquet. The other young man, Henry Bertin, before leaving to join the colours, appealed to his mother not to refuse him permission to go, saying, "I feel I have to go for my country." The action of these brave fellows showed what the young men of Acadia are prepared to do to play their part in the struggle for liberty, right and justice.
The people of Canada have always shown themselves willing and ready to respond to the call of duty. Many outside observers have remarked that the plane of Canadian

patriotism wag the loftiest ever offered to human contemplation by reason of the 'foamy virtues of the different races embraced in the Dominion, races inspired by the highest ideals of Christianity. In the present crisis they have exhibited to the world their readiness to bear the greatest sacrifices for the preservation of those ideals. The fact has 'been dwelt upon that Canada) engaged voluntarily in this war. She went with all the speed possible to the assistance of the Motherland, and of the small nations which were threatened by Piussian militarism. But Canada has not been alone in showing such a fine example. We have seen the same response on the part of our sister dominions. We have seen Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Newfoundland, and other portions of the Empire moving with the harmony which has been the admiration of the world and the consternation of the Kaiser of 'Germany. How is it that Great Britain has been able to evoke the patriotism of all her possessions at the moment of trial? How has she been able to link together her distant possessions, and to present such solidarity in the face of the enemy? All this was accomplished, not by .any threat or menace such as the Kaiser of Germany would use, not by the blood-andiron policy of Bismarck, not by conscription, but through love beaming across the seas and drawing from every British shore ithe affection of Britain's millions of subjects blended inito one common) soull under the ^enevolienit smile of Providence. From Ireland, which has suffered persecution for centuries, we have seen thousands of soldiers instantly respond to the call and take their place in the trenches alongside the Belgian soldiers. The Irish soldier in the battlefield, mindful of the noble words of Gladstone his protector, does not merely look on while the fight for freedom progresses hut rushes into the fray and willingly sacrifices his life. His valour and fearlessness is excelled only by the heroism of the Belgian soldier. Such, Mr. Speaker, is the position in which we are to-day, and which is likely to continue for some time to come. The people of Canada will continue to make any sacrifices that may be needed, sacrifices in men and sacrifices in money.
As I said a moment ago, Britain accomplished all these marvels without conscription, and I wish to say how much I appreciated the declaration of the right hon. the Prime Minister the other day, and the declaration of the leader of the Opposition, 	-
that there shall be no conscription in Canada. Why, Mr. Speaker, we are engaged in this war for the very purpose of effacing, if we can, conscription from the face of the earth. The conscription of the Prussian people has been the cause of all the bloodshed during the last eighty years. It is against this Prussian militarism, which has made a whole nation of seventy million people merely the tools of military officers, that we are sending our young men to-day. The Prussian soldier is fighting today not because he is exercising his own intelligence, nor from any motives of freedom, but to give vent to his passions,-amid patriotism takes second place in his heart.
Canada is to raise five hundred thousand troops. In speaking to the young men of my county I have always said that we wanted them to go voluntarily, that we wanted them to go because we did not want conscription applied to Canada if Germany should unfortunately win this war, and the more deeply our young men have been impressed with this idea the more eagerly have they come forward. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), who knows conditions in New Brunswick, is aware that in the early months of the war recruits in that part of the country came forward rather slowly, for the reason that like nearly every one in Canada and in Great Britain too they made the mistake of thinking the war would be a short one. Many young men have said to me, What is the use oi going? Why, after we have had six months training at Valcartier the war will be over. But now, when the necessity for sacrifice has been made clear to them, they are coming forward in thousands where a year ago they came forward in hundreds. I agree with the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that if conscription is absolutely necessary in Canada we shall have to resort to it, but I maintain that if we adopt the proper measures it will not be necessary to have conscription in order to raise the 250,000 men who are required. The people of Canada will willingly give them. I wish to place myself emphatically on record against conscription. I do not wish to say anything offensive in regard to what has happened in England lately. One of the glories of Britain is that she has never had to resort to conscription. It is cf course only a mild sort of conscription they are proposing there now and merely a temporary measure, because the leading men of Great Britain no doubt feel that they

owe it to the Allies to do all they possibly can to help secure victory. It is to be regretted that a year ago the labour element in Great Britain was not really educated to the necessities of the occasion. We have seen that Welsh statesman, Mr. Lloyd George, appealing to the labour element, and the labour element once it was educated to the necessities of the occasion responded with a patriotism that could not be excelled by any other class of British subjects.
I agree also with the opinion of my hon. friend from Edmonton, that-, our wounded soldiers who return to Canada must receive a larger pension. If you satisfy our young men that if they become incapacitated through the war they will be treated by the nation according to their sacrifice, if you convince them that they are fighting for a nation which is worthy of the sacrifice, and that when they come back incapacitated they will not be at the mercy of any municipality or even a province, but that the Government of the nation itself will give them an adequate pension-and they have a right to it having sacrificed the'ir future and exposed their life

then I say, we shall get all the recruits we need.
The duty of providing for our wounded soldiers ought not to be left to the provinces nor to the Patriotic Fund. Our soldiers must feel their security before they go. The provinces should not have such a burden imposed upon them, because some of our provinces have certainly no great wealth at theiir disposal. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) will agree with me, I am sure, when I say that the revenues of the province of New Brunswick are small compared with all its necessities, and if we were to impose to-day upon the Government of that province the responsibility, or a part of the responsibility, for the maintenance of our returned soldiers, some of them might not get the comforts which they have a right to expect. The Dominion Government and the nation at large should undertake this duty. The same thing has been done in the United States. The Government )of the United States after the war of the Revolution did not distribute the cost of the pensions to her returned soldiers amongst the different States nor leave it to the devotion of her people, but established a pension board and gave the soldier what was needed for his comfort and that of his family when he got back from the front.
Another question which I wish to bring
to the attention of the House is a paragraph in the speech from the Throne which reads as follows:
The life of the present Parliament expires in the autumn of this year, and, under existing legislation, a dissolution and election would be necessary in the early future. My advisers, however, are of the opinion that the wishes of the Canadian people and the present requirements of the war would he best met my avoiding the distraction and confusion consequent upon a general election at so critical a time.
That purpose can only be effected through the medium of legislation by the Parliament of the United Kingdom. A resolution authorizing and requesting the enactment of such legislation as will extend the life of this Parliament for the period of one year will he presented to you.
No one appreciates more deeply than I do the position in which Canada is at present on account of this war. It has been said by the Liberal party at least that the Government of the day should carry on the prosecution of the war. Now, the war has lasted eighteen months, and is not yet ended, and while the end may come within a short time, the war may, unfortunately, last a very long time. The proposal in the speech from the Throne means an amendment to the British North America Act under which we live to-day, and I view it with all sincerity and seriousness. My views upon the constitution of Canada have been well known to this House. I believe, since I have been a member of it, and also to the people of my constituency, either through my addresses to the public or through the press, for many years before I became a member of this House. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows that I always view with apprehension any suggestion of a change in the constitution of Canada. While the minority in New Brunswick have suffered on account of the constitution, we have been educated to suffer for the sake of the constitution, in order that changes in it and in the methods of applying its principles may not endanger privileges conferred upon some classes of the people by it. Our constitution is not exactly the same as that of Great Britain: it is the depository of the privileges of the minorities throughout the whole Dominion.
